My grandfather sharpened his knives on a belt sander he'd bolted to the workbench sometime in the seventies, and the whole garage smelled like hot metal when he did it. You could hear the machine from the driveway. That was your warning to knock instead of walking in, because he'd be leaning into the spark stream with his reading glasses on, deaf to everything.

He was not a gentle man, exactly, but he was careful. There's a difference. Gentle people apologize for taking up space. Careful people just pay attention to where the edges are. He kept his chisels in a canvas roll his brother had brought back from Korea, each pocket numbered in laundry marker, and if you borrowed one you put it back in the right pocket or you didn't borrow another one.

The summer I turned twelve he taught me to sharpen a mower blade. The trick, he said, is that you're not making it sharp. You're making it even. Sharp happens on its own once the edge is straight enough to agree with itself. I have thought about that sentence at odd moments for thirty years, usually while doing some task he would have found overcomplicated. He died with every tool he ever owned still in working order, which I suppose was the point.
